mcqs.question: Why does Bellman-Ford relax every edge for exactly V-1 rounds?
options: Because V-1 is the number of edges in the graph
V-1 is an arbitrary convention with no deeper justification
Fewer rounds would make the algorithm run faster than Dijkstra
A simple shortest path in a graph with no negative cycle uses at most V-1 edges, and each full round propagates distance information one edge further along any path
mcqs.explanation: Since a simple path can't revisit a node, its maximum possible length is V-1 edges — and each complete round of relaxing every edge guarantees that any true shortest path's information advances by one more edge, so V-1 rounds are exactly enough to fully propagate even the longest possible shortest path. V-1 has no relation to the actual edge count, and it's not simply an arbitrary choice.

mcqs.question: After running Bellman-Ford's normal V-1 rounds, an extra Vth round of edge relaxation still finds an improvement. What does this indicate?
options: The graph simply needs more rounds and V-1 was an underestimate for this specific graph
The graph has more than one connected component
The source node was chosen incorrectly
A negative cycle reachable from the source exists — the improvement can't come from a legitimate simple path, since those are fully propagated within V-1 rounds
mcqs.explanation: V-1 rounds are provably sufficient to fully propagate any distance improvement along a genuine simple (cycle-free) shortest path — if something still improves beyond that, the only remaining explanation is a negative cycle being looped, which makes shortest-path distances undefined for anything reachable through it. This isn't about needing more rounds in general, source choice, or component count; it's specifically the negative-cycle signature.

mcqs.question: In Floyd-Warshall, what does dist[i][j] represent after the algorithm has processed intermediate node k = 5 (out of, say, 10 total nodes)?
options: The shortest path from i to j using only nodes 1 through 5 as possible intermediate stops
The shortest path from i to j using at least 5 edges
The final, fully correct shortest path from i to j, regardless of k
The distance from node 5 to both i and j combined
mcqs.explanation: The DP's defining invariant is that after processing k, dist[i][j] reflects the shortest i-to-j path allowed to route through any of nodes 1 through k as intermediate stops — not a statement about edge count, and not the final answer until k has reached every node. It has nothing to do with a distance involving node 5 specifically as an endpoint.

mcqs.question: In the Floyd-Warshall triple loop, why must k be the OUTERMOST loop rather than i or j?
options: Loop order is purely a style choice and has no effect on the result
Making k outermost is only needed to improve cache performance, not correctness

Each full pass over k must finalize 'shortest paths using intermediates 1..k' across the entire matrix before k increases, since later comparisons depend on dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] already reflecting all previous k values
k must be outermost only when the graph has negative weights
mcqs.explanation: The DP recurrence assumes dist[i][k] and dist[k][j] already incorporate every intermediate up to k-1 by the time they're used to update dist[i][j] for the current k — swapping the loop order breaks that dependency and produces incorrect results, not just slower ones. This is a correctness requirement of the algorithm's structure, independent of cache effects or edge weight signs.

mcqs.question: You need shortest-path distances from 3 specific source nodes in a large, sparse graph with 50,000 nodes, all non-negative weights. What's the most efficient standard approach?
options: Run Dijkstra's algorithm 3 times, once per required source
Floyd-Warshall once, since it computes all pairs and you can just read off the 3 rows you need
Bellman-Ford once per source, since it's guaranteed correct for any weight configuration
Floyd-Warshall is required whenever more than one source is needed
mcqs.explanation: With non-negative weights and only 3 sources needed (not all 50,000), running Dijkstra 3 times costs roughly 3 x O((V+E) log V), while Floyd-Warshall's O(V^3) at this scale is computationally infeasible — a massive overpay for information mostly never used. Bellman-Ford would work but is strictly slower than Dijkstra when negative weights aren't a concern, and multiple sources don't require an all-pairs algorithm at all.

mcqs.question: An implementation runs Bellman-Ford's V-1 relaxation rounds correctly but skips the extra Vth-round negative-cycle check. On a graph WITH a negative cycle reachable from the source, what happens?
options: The algorithm throws a clear error about the negative cycle
It returns distance values as if they were correct, with nothing signaling that they're meaningless given the negative cycle
The V-1 rounds alone are already sufficient to guarantee correctness even with a negative cycle present
The algorithm automatically extends to more rounds until it converges
mcqs.explanation: V-1 rounds alone produce output regardless of whether a negative cycle exists, but that output is only meaningful when no negative cycle is present — without the extra check, the algorithm silently returns numbers with no signal that 'shortest path' isn't even well-defined for the affected nodes. There's no automatic error, no self-correcting extension, and V-1 rounds do not guarantee correctness in the presence of a negative cycle.
